title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 46
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Getting the Smoke Out
passages.text:
A. For most of history a fire indoors meant smoke indoors. A hearth in the middle of a floor, with a hole in the roof above it, heats a room efficiently because the heat is released where the people are, and it fills that room with everything else the fire produces. The chimney is often described as an improvement in heating and was in fact a considerable step backwards in it, adopted for reasons that had nothing to do with warmth.

B. What the chimney permitted was the division of the house. A central hearth requires a single tall space open to the roof so the smoke can rise and disperse, which means one room; a flue against a wall allows an upper floor, separate rooms, and a fire in more than one of them. The private chamber, and the social arrangement that goes with it, is a consequence of a change in how smoke was handled.

C. The thermal cost was substantial and took centuries to address. A fire venting into a flue draws air from the room to burn, and that air is replaced by cold air drawn in through every gap in the building, so a chimney simultaneously removes heat up the flue and pulls a draught across the floor. Improvements narrowed the throat, brought the fire forward and shaped the back to reflect heat, and each of these was a correction to a problem the design had introduced.

D. The enclosed stove was a better answer and spread unevenly for reasons of culture rather than physics. A closed metal or masonry box burns fuel more completely, releases heat gradually into the room and loses far less up the flue, and it was adopted widely in some regions and resisted in others where an open fire was valued for the sight of it. The visible flame was worth a measurable quantity of fuel to the people choosing.

E. Smoke indoors remains one of the largest environmental health problems in the world and is barely visible in public discussion. Cooking on open fires or simple stoves in unventilated spaces exposes very large numbers of people, mostly women and young children, to concentrations that would close a workplace anywhere else, and the resulting illness is attributed to poverty in general rather than to a specific and solvable cause.

F. Improved stove programmes have a long record of failure that is instructive rather than discouraging. Designs that performed well in testing were not used, or were used alongside the old fire rather than instead of it, because they cooked more slowly, would not take the local pot, could not be repaired locally, or cost money that had other claims on it. The programmes that worked were the ones that treated the cook as the customer rather than the beneficiary.

passages.title: The Plants That Took Over
passages.text:
Grasses are a young family that now covers something approaching a third of the land surface, and their success is built on a single structural decision. Most plants grow from the tips of their shoots, so an animal that eats the top of a plant removes its growing point; grasses grow from the base of the leaf instead, which means the part an animal eats is the part the plant was going to discard. A grazed grass is not damaged in the way a grazed shrub is.

That arrangement made a partnership possible that reshaped whole continents. Large grazing animals suppress the tree seedlings that would otherwise shade grasses out, and grasses tolerate the grazing that suppresses their competitors, so grassland and grazing herds sustain one another in a way neither could sustain alone. Remove the grazers and much grassland becomes woodland; remove the grass and the herds cannot be supported.

Fire performs the same service and grasses are equally well suited to it. A fire moving through dry grass removes standing dead material and kills woody seedlings while leaving growing points at or below ground level intact, and regrowth from those points is rapid because the root systems survive. Many grasslands are maintained by burning, and where burning stops, the boundary with woodland moves.

The chemical defence is minerals rather than poison. Grasses accumulate silica in their tissues, which wears down the teeth of animals that eat them, and the response among grazing mammals was the evolution of high-crowned teeth that can withstand a lifetime of abrasion. This is a plainly visible arms race preserved in the fossil record, and the spread of grasslands can be traced in the changing teeth of the animals that lived alongside them.

Human dependence on this family is close to total and rarely noticed. Wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, sorghum, millet and sugar cane are all grasses, and they supply the majority of the calories humans consume directly, plus most of what is fed to the animals people eat. An agricultural system is in large part a managed grassland, and the crops in it retain the properties that made the family successful in the wild.

The carbon story is where recent attention has concentrated and where the claims need care. Grassland stores most of its carbon below ground in roots and soil rather than above ground in wood, which makes it more resistant to fire and drought than forest carbon and harder to measure, easier to lose through ploughing, and slow to rebuild. The storage is real and substantial; the confident numbers attached to grassland restoration schemes are considerably less secure than the underlying fact.

passages.title: Giving It Away
passages.text:
Charitable giving is studied more than most economic behaviour and understood less well than the volume of research suggests. People give in patterns that pure altruism does not predict: donations respond strongly to being asked, to who else is giving, to whether the gift is visible, and to a single identified beneficiary rather than to statistics about many. Something real is happening, and it is not simply the purchase of outcomes for others.

The identifiable victim effect is the most reliably demonstrated of these patterns and the most awkward. People give substantially more to one named individual than to a group, and giving falls when the individual is presented alongside the numbers describing the wider problem, so adding accurate information about scale reduces the response. An appeal optimised for money raised and an appeal optimised for conveying the size of a problem are different appeals.

Overhead is the metric on which donors have been most systematically misled, largely by the sector itself. Administration and fundraising costs are treated as waste to be minimised, so organisations compete to report low ratios, and the pressure produces underinvestment in the evaluation, systems and staff that determine whether the work is any good. A charity that spends nothing on measuring its results reports an excellent ratio and cannot tell you whether it helps anyone.

The effectiveness movement made a genuine contribution and has a real limitation. Comparing interventions by cost per unit of benefit exposed enormous differences between charities addressing similar problems, and directing money towards the demonstrably effective has produced measurable good. What the approach handles poorly is everything whose value resists that measurement — advocacy, cultural institutions, long-horizon research, and organisations working on problems where the counterfactual cannot be established.

Large-scale private philanthropy raises a question that is about power rather than money. A foundation directing sums comparable to a public budget makes decisions about schooling, health or research that affect many people without any of the accountability attached to public spending, and its funds usually carry tax advantages, which means the public has contributed to a programme it did not choose. This is a reasonable objection and it applies whether or not the programme is a good one.

What the evidence supports most clearly is unglamorous. Regular, unrestricted, long-term funding lets an organisation plan, retain staff and abandon what is not working; restricted grants for specific projects, renewed annually and requiring separate reporting, consume a large share of what they provide. Donors who want to be useful have a more reliable lever in how they give than in refining what they give to.
